interviews.author: andreas-malm
interviews.reaction: Damaging fossil fuel machinery is legitimate as long as no person is harmed. Most movements that won had a militant flank that damaged property. Ruling sabotage out on principle leaves fossil capital free to ignore polite protest while emissions keep rising.

interviews.author: bill-mckibben
interviews.reaction: The urgency is real, since the planet has already changed. But the industry loses its power when it loses public consent. Mass, open campaigns like the Keystone XL fight and divestment drain that consent. Sabotage narrows the movement when breadth matters most.

interviews.author: michael-shellenberger
interviews.reaction: Damaging fossil fuel infrastructure is not legitimate climate action. It makes energy scarcer and costlier, and the poor pay first. It feeds on apocalyptic fear. Emissions fall when cleaner, denser energy such as nuclear replaces fossil fuels, not when supply is destroyed.

interviews.author: arne-naess
interviews.reaction: Open, nonviolent direct action that puts bodies in the way and accepts the penalty is legitimate. Secret sabotage is not, because means and ends cannot be separated. Hidden damage hardens conflict, treats opponents as enemies, and leaves the worldview behind the pipeline untouched.

interviews.author: ken-saro-wiwa
interviews.reaction: Oil extraction is itself ecological war on peoples whose land, water and air were taken without consent. The legitimate answer is open, nonviolent mass organizing for rights and resource control, because sabotage gives repressive regimes a pretext and the villages pay for it.

interviews.author: francoise-deaubonne
interviews.reaction: Fossil infrastructure belongs to the same patriarchal power that seized the fertility of women and of the earth, so striking it is legitimate defence of life. It is only legitimate when women lead it and it serves a full change of the system, not property damage alone.

interviews.author: roger-scruton
interviews.reaction: Sabotage replaces law and consent with the will of a self-appointed few, and the resentment it breeds weakens the love of home that sustains lasting stewardship. Open defence of a place by the people who live there has some standing, but distant wrecking does not.

interviews.author: william-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: Sabotage works like an arbitrary tax on a few emitters, set by whoever does the wrecking and unrelated to the damage carbon does. A carbon price that covers every emission and rises along an optimal path cuts emissions lastingly. Disruption only moves them elsewhere.

interviews.author: jacques-ellul
interviews.reaction: Sabotage hits one link in a technological system that repairs itself and responds with more surveillance and security technique. Choosing a means for its efficiency stays inside the logic it opposes. Refusing what the system demands in daily life goes further.

interviews.author: murray-bookchin
interviews.reaction: Qualified opposition. Ecological damage is rooted in social hierarchy, so secret sabotage by small groups misses the root and builds no power from below. Direct action becomes legitimate when citizens' assemblies decide it openly, as one step toward municipal power that replaces fossil rule.

interviews.author: joan-martinez-alier
interviews.reaction: Resistance to extraction by affected communities is an ecological distribution conflict and a form of environmentalism, not a crime against the climate. Legitimacy depends on who bears the harm and who decides. The record does not address covert sabotage, so it is judged only by analogy.

interviews.author: giorgos-kallis
interviews.reaction: Damage to fossil infrastructure can be legitimate if it belongs to a broad movement building democratic, collective self-limitation of extraction. It cannot replace that choice. Lasting limits are set by a free society, not forced on it by a few.

interviews.author: nicole-seymour
interviews.reaction: The work does not address sabotage, so this is reasoning by analogy. Legitimacy is the wrong test. Ecological action should be judged by whether it widens who cares. Solemn, heroic sabotage risks repeating the movement's gloom and sanctimony.

interviews.author: bill-devall
interviews.reaction: Open, nonviolent damage to machines that destroy living places can be defended, as long as no person is harmed and the penalty is accepted. Sabotage alone remains a reform tactic, because the real target is the worldview that treats nature as a resource.

interviews.author: naomi-klein
interviews.reaction: Blocking mines, pipelines and wells with bodies, lawsuits and Indigenous rights claims is legitimate resistance, because markets and governments have failed. The work says little about damaging property. Legitimacy comes from a broad movement that wins a just transition, not from secret sabotage.

interviews.author: starhawk
interviews.reaction: Open, collective direct action against fossil infrastructure, such as blockades, is legitimate because it builds shared power. Secret sabotage by a few tends to reproduce power-over, through hierarchy and closed decisions, so it is not clearly legitimate.

interviews.author: chico-mendes
interviews.reaction: Collective, open blockades by people defending their own livelihood are legitimate. Secret damage to machines by a few people turns potential allies among poor workers into enemies and invites repression. Legitimacy comes from mass action led by the community whose life is at stake.

interviews.author: pascal-bruckner
interviews.reaction: Sabotage follows from catastrophism. Once collapse is preached as imminent, any means seems justified, and ecology becomes a morality of penance that punishes ordinary people through scarce, costly energy. Progress and abundance, not fanaticism, reduce emissions.

interviews.author: robyn-eckersley
interviews.reaction: Opposed as a strategy, though the grievance is granted. Ecological legitimacy comes from decisions answerable to all affected, including future generations. Sabotage goes around the state instead of transforming it. Affected communities defending their own land have stronger standing than distant saboteurs do.

interviews.author: hans-jonas
interviews.reaction: The threat to human life on Earth makes the urgency real, but responsibility puts the worst case first. Sabotage has uncertain effects and can escalate, so it gambles with the future it claims to protect. Restraint through collective policy has priority.

interviews.author: pope-francis
interviews.reaction: The urgency is real and the poor bear the harm of extraction. Secret damage to infrastructure still fails as a method. It rarely brings ecological conversion, it puts its costs and the repression that follows on the vulnerable, and it trusts too much in control. Open, community-led resistance and dialogue are better.

interviews.author: nnimmo-bassey
interviews.reaction: The infrastructure of extraction already damages Africa twice, through spills and flares on the ground and through the warming it feeds. Legitimacy should be judged by who bears the harm. Action led by affected communities carries more weight than sabotage by distant actors.

interviews.author: erik-swyngedouw
interviews.reaction: Consensual, expert-managed climate policy leaves the economic order beyond debate. Acts that break this consensus can reopen the choice between different worlds, so they can be legitimate as political antagonism rather than management. The 2010 work does not address sabotage directly.

interviews.author: luc-ferry
interviews.reaction: Opposed, by analogy from humanist ecology: nature has value for free human beings, not rights against them. Sabotage puts the conviction of a few in place of democratic deliberation, so environmental protection must come through law and persuasion.
